p: Welcome to the first lesson of the course. Before we meet Cognac, whisky or rum, we need the map that explains them all. In this lesson we look at the four steps that every spirit goes through, at the difference between fermentation and distillation, and at the two kinds of still that distillers use: the pot still and the column still. Once these ideas are clear, almost every bottle on a bar shelf starts to make sense.

So, what is a spirit? Put simply, it is an alcoholic drink whose strength has been raised by distillation. But distillation is only one part of the story. Every spirit, from the lightest vodka to the oldest brandy, follows the same four steps. First, the raw material is prepared. Second, it is fermented. Third, it is distilled. And fourth, the producer decides what happens after distillation. That fourth step has a lesson of its own, the next one. Today we focus on the first three.

Step one: preparing the raw material. The goal is simple: to obtain a sugary liquid, because without sugar there can be no fermentation. The raw material must come from a plant. In theory any plant will do, but in practice only a handful are used, such as grapes, grains, sugar cane, agave and potatoes. Some, like grapes or sugar cane, already contain sugar that is easy to extract. Others, like grains, contain no sugar at all and must be processed to create it. And each raw material gives the spirit its own family of aromas.

Step two: fermentation. Here a tiny living organism does the work: yeast. Yeast is added to the sugary liquid and feeds on the sugar. In return it produces two things: ethanol, the alcohol the distiller is after, and carbon dioxide, a gas that simply escapes as waste. When fermentation is over, the liquid usually contains between eight and ten percent alcohol by volume, roughly the strength of a strong beer. And yeast gives a bonus: it creates new aromas, especially fruity ones.

A quick word on that expression, alcohol by volume. It tells you what share of a liquid is alcohol. If a spirit is forty percent alcohol by volume, then forty percent of what is in the glass is pure alcohol and the rest is mostly water. You will hear this measure throughout the course, so it is worth getting comfortable with it now.

Step three: distillation, the step that actually creates a spirit. Its aim is to concentrate the alcohol made during fermentation. The trick relies on one simple fact: alcohol boils at a lower temperature than water. So when the fermented liquid is heated to boiling, the vapours that rise contain a higher proportion of alcohol than the liquid left behind. These vapours are collected and cooled, and they turn back into a liquid that is stronger than the one we started with. Here is the key idea: fermentation makes the alcohol, distillation concentrates it.

How strong is a spirit when it first comes off the still? Anywhere from about sixty to ninety-six percent. And this strength matters enormously for flavour. The lower the distillation strength, the more intense the aromas. The higher the strength, the fewer aromas survive. At ninety-six percent there is so little aroma left that the spirit is called neutral. Picture a radio playing in a noisy room: the louder the alcohol, the fainter the music of the aromas.

Now the stills. There are two types: pot stills and column stills. There are hundreds of designs, but each type has features in common. A pot still has three parts: a pot sitting on a heat source, a condenser that is kept cold, and a pipe linking the two. The liquid boils in the pot, the vapours climb up and pass into the condenser, often a coiled tube sitting in cold water, where they turn back into liquid. The stills used for Cognac are heated by gas burners; most modern pot stills use steam.

The pot still works in batches. Think of a washing machine: you load it, run the cycle, then empty it and clean it before the next load. It cannot run continuously. And one pass is not enough to make a spirit, so most distillers who use pot stills distil twice. This is called double pot still distillation. The fermented liquid starts at about ten percent; after the first distillation it is about twenty-five percent; after the second, about seventy-five. The result is a fairly low-strength spirit, with medium to pronounced aromas and plenty of character and complexity.

The pot still has two limits: it works one batch at a time, and it can never make a very strong spirit, say ninety percent or more, however many times you distil. The answer to both problems was the column still. It is a tall, vertical structure divided into sections. Hot alcoholic vapour enters at the bottom and rises, while liquid runs down. In effect, many distillations are stacked on top of one another, all happening at once. The higher the vapour climbs, the stronger it becomes, and the spirit leaves near the top. Because it never has to be emptied, a column still runs continuously and quickly.

Not all columns give the same result, and this is a favourite exam trap. A short column with few sections makes a lower-strength spirit with medium or pronounced aromas, quite close to a pot still spirit. A tall column with many sections reaches high strengths and gives a light spirit. And the tallest columns, with the most sections, reach ninety-five or ninety-six percent and produce a neutral spirit. So remember: a column still does not automatically mean a light spirit. Its height, and the strength it reaches, decide.

Here is a memory tip. Think of the pot still as a lift and the column still as an escalator. The lift stops, opens, empties and starts again: that is batch distillation, slower, but it carries plenty of flavour. The escalator never stops: that is continuous distillation, and the higher it climbs, the lighter the spirit becomes.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, every spirit follows four steps: prepare the raw material, ferment it, distil it, and finish it after distillation. Second, fermentation makes the alcohol, at around eight to ten percent, and distillation concentrates it: the lower the distillation strength, the more flavour remains. Third, the pot still works in batches and gives low-strength, flavourful spirits, while the column still runs continuously and, depending on its height, gives anything from flavourful to light or completely neutral spirits.

In the last lesson we followed a spirit up to the moment it leaves the still. Now we look at what gives it its flavour, its sweetness and its colour. We will see where aromas come from, what oak does, why producers blend, how other flavours can be added, where sweetness and colour really come from, and why almost every spirit meets water before it is bottled. This fourth step is where two very similar spirits can end up worlds apart.

First, flavour. It is built in layers. The raw material lays the foundation: grapes bring fruity and floral notes, barley brings cereal notes, agave brings herbal and peppery ones. Fermentation then adds more aromas, mostly fruity, created by the yeast. Finally, distillation decides how much of all this survives. Distil to a low strength and the aromas stay intense; distil to a very high strength and they almost disappear. Think of three sieves, one after the other, each letting more or less character through.

Now a fact that surprises many people: every spirit leaves the still colourless and dry, meaning it contains no sugar at all. Whatever colour or sweetness you find later was added afterwards. So the aim of this fourth step is to adjust colour, aroma, sweetness and strength to suit the style being made. There are three broad paths: the spirit can stay unaged, it can be aged in oak, or it can be flavoured with something other than oak. Often the law makes the choice: Scotch whisky must be aged in oak, while Tequila may be aged or left unaged.

Let's start with unaged spirits. To keep the clear look and the aromas that came off the still, the producer stores the spirit for a short time in stainless steel tanks. Steel is like a blank sheet of paper: it gives nothing and takes nothing. These spirits can still be sweetened or have their strength adjusted, and colour can even be added just before bottling, as we will see in a moment.

Oak ageing, also called maturation, is a very different story. The spirit rests in oak barrels, usually for years, and the wood adds both colour and aroma. The colour follows a set sequence: first lemon, then gold, then amber and, in very rare cases, brown. How much colour the spirit picks up depends on two things: the barrel and the time. A newer barrel and a longer stay give a deeper colour.

Oak also brings aromas: vanilla, cinnamon, cloves and coconut. A new barrel, one that has never been used, gives the most. Once a barrel has been emptied and filled again, it is called an old barrel, and it gives less aroma. With every use it gives a little less again, just like a tea bag dipped in a second and then a third cup. So a producer who wants a bold oak imprint chooses new barrels, and one who wants a gentle touch chooses old ones.

Time adds something else. During maturation, some water and some alcohol slowly evaporate through the wood, so what remains in the barrel becomes more concentrated. And after a very long time, often decades, new aromas appear: fruit cake, dried fruit, leather and wood polish. These add layer upon layer of complexity, which is why a very old spirit seems to keep revealing something new.

Next comes blending, a key stage for oak-aged spirits. No two barrels are exactly alike, even if they were filled with the same spirit on the same day. The blender's job is to combine the contents of many barrels into batches for a brand, and there are two aims. The first is consistency: people expect the same bottle to taste the same every time. The second is complexity: an extraordinary single barrel is rare, so the easiest way to build depth is to mix spirits with different characters. The more types of spirit a blender has to work with, the easier this becomes.

Some spirits are flavoured with something other than oak, such as fruits, seeds, herbs and spices. There are three main techniques. Redistillation: the spirit is distilled again with these ingredients, giving a flavoured but colourless spirit. Maceration: the ingredients soak in the spirit, like a cold herbal tea, and give it flavour and colour. Or ready-made flavourings are simply added. We will come back to all of this in the lesson on flavoured spirits.

Now sweetness. Since every spirit leaves the still dry, any sweetness you taste was added later, and in most cases it is simply sugar. Be careful with the word: in this course, sweet means the taste of sugar on the palate, nothing else. A Bourbon, for example, has vanilla and fruity aromas that people often call sweet, yet it has no added sugar. It is dry. A sweet smell and a sweet taste are not the same thing.

And colour. Oak is the most obvious source. Then there is caramel colour. Because barrels give different shades, blenders sometimes add a very small amount of caramel so that every batch looks the same. Used correctly, caramel colour is not sweet and adds no aroma. Some spirits get all or nearly all of their colour from it, so even an unaged spirit can be deeply coloured. Finally, other natural or artificial colourings are used too, especially in liqueurs, sometimes in very bright shades.

The very last step before bottling is dilution. The vast majority of spirits are brought down to forty percent alcohol by volume by adding completely pure water. Why? To make them drinkable: very high alcohol numbs the palate, so you could neither taste nor enjoy the spirit. This pure water adds no flavour; it only lowers the strength.

Here is the memorable tip for this lesson: colour is not proof of age, and a sweet smell is not proof of sugar. A dark spirit may owe its colour to caramel rather than to years in oak, and a dry spirit may smell of vanilla and fruit. When in doubt, ask how the spirit was made.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, flavour comes from the raw material, from fermentation and from distillation strength, and every newly made spirit is colourless and dry. Second, after the still a spirit can stay unaged in steel, be aged in new or old oak, which adds colour and aromas, or be flavoured; blending brings consistency and complexity. Third, sweetness always comes from added sugar, colour comes from oak, caramel or other colourings, and most spirits are diluted with pure water to forty percent.

Welcome to our first spirit family: grape brandy. A grape brandy is, quite simply, a wine that has been distilled, and the best known of all is Cognac, from south-west France. In this lesson we follow Cognac through the four steps we already know: where its grapes come from and how they become wine, why the law insists on pot stills, what oak and blending bring, and the three age terms you will find on the label.

Step one, the raw material. Cognac must be made from grapes grown in a specific part of south-west France, north of the town of Bordeaux. Grapes from anywhere else cannot become Cognac, however carefully they are distilled. So the name is not a recipe that can be copied: it is an address. These grapes give Cognac its basic character, with fruity and floral aromas that you will still recognise in the glass years later.

Grapes are an easy raw material to work with, because their juice is already full of sugar. There is no need for complicated processing, as there is with grain. The grapes are simply pressed to release their juice. Picture a bunch of grapes on its way to becoming a bottle of wine: Cognac starts down exactly the same road.

Step two, fermentation. The sugary juice is fermented straight away, and the yeast turns its sugar into alcohol. The result is a wine. And this is the point to remember: what goes into the still is not grape juice and not grapes, but wine. Before it becomes Cognac, every drop of it has been wine. Halfway along the road, instead of heading for a glass, our bunch of grapes takes the turning towards the still.

Step three, distillation. For Cognac the law leaves no choice: the wine must be distilled twice in a pot still. Column stills are not allowed. As we saw earlier, the pot still works in batches: after each distillation it has to be emptied and cleaned before it can be filled again. It is slow and labour-intensive. The traditional Cognac still is heated by gas burners, and its condenser is a coiled tube sitting in cold water that is constantly refreshed.

Why insist on so much effort? Because a pot still produces a spirit of relatively low strength, packed with flavour and character. That is exactly what Cognac needs: the fruity and floral aromas of the grapes carry through into the spirit instead of being stripped away. You could say that double distillation in a pot still protects the soul of the wine. It is the same reason pot stills are chosen for other characterful spirits too.

Step four, what happens after distillation. Fresh from the still, the spirit is colourless and cannot yet be called Cognac. The law says it must spend at least two years in oak barrels first. That time in wood gives Cognac its colour and adds aromas of vanilla and toast. Two years is only the minimum, though, and many Cognacs rest for much longer.

The finest Cognacs are aged for many years. As some water and alcohol evaporate through the wood, the spirit becomes very concentrated, and new aromas slowly develop: fruit cake, leather and wood polish. These are the signs of a long and patient maturation. If you ever smell a very old Cognac, try to find those three notes: they are the fingerprint of time. Then comes blending. Nearly all Cognacs are blends, made by combining spirits of different ages. Younger spirits bring freshness and fruit, older ones bring depth, and together they create extra complexity. The blender also aims for consistency, so that each bottle tastes like the last.

Before dilution and bottling, there are two more common touches. It is quite usual for producers to add a little caramel colour, to keep the shade the same from batch to batch, and to sweeten their Cognac slightly. Then, as with most spirits, it is diluted with pure water and bottled. So a Cognac can feel gently rounded on the palate, even though it left the still completely dry.

Now the age terms, which are a favourite exam topic. Cognacs are grouped by age, and three labelling terms matter. Each one guarantees the age of the youngest spirit in the blend. VS means the youngest spirit is at least two years old. VSOP means at least four years. XO means at least ten years. Older spirits may be in the blend too, but the label always speaks for the youngest.

Here is the tip for this lesson. Think of a staircase with three steps: two, four and ten. And remember that the youngest spirit sets the step. Imagine a blend of a five-year-old spirit and a twenty-year-old spirit. The twenty-year-old does not count for the label: the youngest is five, so the blend can be called VSOP, but not XO.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Cognac is a grape brandy from a defined area north of Bordeaux; the grapes are pressed and the juice is fermented straight away into wine. Second, the law requires double distillation in a pot still, which gives a low-strength spirit full of flavour. Third, Cognac must spend at least two years in oak, most Cognacs are blends, often with a little caramel and sugar, and the age terms are VS for two years, VSOP for four and XO for ten, always counting the youngest spirit.

In this lesson we meet vodka, the most widely mixed spirit behind any bar, and in many ways the opposite of the Cognac we have just studied. We will see what it can be made from, where it can be made, the one thing that really defines it, how it is finished after distillation, and the two styles you are likely to meet: the fully neutral vodka and the vodka that keeps a little character.

Let's start with the big idea. With Cognac, almost everything is fixed: the place, the grape, the type of still. With vodka, almost nothing is. Vodka can be made anywhere in the world, and it can be made from any raw material. So what makes a spirit a vodka? Not the country, and not the plant. It is the strength to which it is distilled. Keep that in mind and the rest of the lesson falls into place.

Step one, the raw material. Any plant-based raw material can be used, but some are traditionally linked with premium-quality vodka. These are grains, especially barley, wheat and rye, and potatoes. Whatever is chosen, it first has to be turned into a sugary liquid, because yeast needs sugar to work. Grains and potatoes are full of starch rather than sugar, so they must be processed first, much as we will see for whisky.

Step two, fermentation. Once the sugary liquid is ready, yeast is added and fermentation takes place, exactly as for every other spirit. The yeast turns the sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide, and it creates some fruity aromas too. But for vodka, most of those aromas are not destined to last, because of what happens next.

Step three, distillation, the heart of vodka. Vodka is a diluted neutral spirit. To count as neutral, a spirit must be distilled to at least ninety-five or ninety-six percent alcohol by volume. Which of the two depends on the law of the country where it is produced. Such a high strength can only be reached in a column still, the tall kind with many sections. Some producers do use pot stills for part of the process, but a pot still alone could never reach neutral strength.

Why the word neutral? Remember the rule from our first lessons: the higher the distillation strength, the fewer aromas survive. At ninety-five or ninety-six percent, a spirit has virtually no flavour left. The fruity notes of fermentation and most of the character of the raw material have been left behind in the still. That is not a fault: for vodka, it is the goal.

Step four, after distillation. Vodka is not aged in oak, so it gets no colour and no aromas from wood. It stays unaged and clear. It is then diluted with pure water down to bottling strength, typically forty percent alcohol by volume. That is why we call it a diluted neutral spirit: neutral when it leaves the still, diluted before it reaches the bottle.

That same neutral spirit has another life, too. As we will see in the lesson on flavoured spirits, most gins, flavoured vodkas and liqueurs start from neutral spirit diluted with water, the very same base that becomes vodka. So understanding vodka also opens the door to a large part of the bar shelf.

Now the styles. Most vodka is made to be as neutral as possible, and this neutrality is exactly what has made it so popular. In mixed drinks and cocktails it adds alcohol without imposing its own flavour, so juices, sodas and liqueurs stay centre stage. Think of it as a blank canvas: the bartender paints on it with other ingredients.

Some vodkas, however, keep a little character. On the nose and on the palate you may notice faint hints of the raw material, such as a touch of grain or of potato. These flavours remain very light compared with those of a whisky or a brandy, and these vodkas are still correctly described as neutral. The difference is subtle, a bit like the difference between two still mineral waters tasted side by side.

Watch out for a few classic exam traps. Vodka does not have to be made from potatoes, nor from grain: any raw material is allowed. It does not have to come from any particular country. It cannot be made to neutral strength in a pot still alone. And it is unaged, not matured in oak. Here is the tip for this lesson: for vodka, think strength, not place and not plant. If you remember that a vodka is defined by being distilled to neutral strength, ninety-five or ninety-six percent, you can answer almost any question about it.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, vodka can be made anywhere, from any raw material, although grains such as barley, wheat and rye, and potatoes, are linked with premium vodka. Second, it is a neutral spirit distilled to at least ninety-five or ninety-six percent in a column still, then left unaged and diluted, typically to forty percent. Third, most vodka is as neutral as possible, which makes it so versatile in cocktails, while some keep faint hints of their raw material and are still called neutral.

Welcome to the world of whisky, spelled with or without an e depending on where it comes from. In this lesson we focus on Scotland. We will see how hard, dry grain is turned into a sugary liquid, the rules that every Scotch whisky must follow, what makes a Single Malt, where the famous smoky flavour comes from, and how Blended Scotch is built from two very different kinds of whisky.

First, what is a whisky? It is an oak-aged spirit that must be made from grains. A handy way to picture it is as distilled beer: grain, water and yeast make a kind of beer, and the still does the rest. Whisky is made all over the world, but the best-known examples come from Scotland, the United States, Ireland, Canada and Japan. Each grain leaves its own mark: barley gives cereal aromas, corn gives sweetcorn aromas, and rye gives spicy, peppery aromas.

Grains pose a problem, though. They are dry and hard, and they are full of starch rather than sugar. Yeast cannot ferment starch, so it has to be converted into sugar first. The classic method is clever, because it lets the barley do almost all of the work itself. It starts with a process called malting.

In malting, the barley grains are allowed to start growing. As they grow, they create natural substances called enzymes, tiny tools that are able to turn starch into sugar. At just the right moment, hot air is used to stop the growth. From now on the grain is called malted barley. It carries its own tools, but it has not used them yet.

Next, the malted barley is crushed into a rough flour, and other crushed grains can be added at this point too. Everything is mixed with warm water, and in this bath the enzymes made by the barley get to work, converting the starch into sugar. The result is a sugary liquid, ready for the yeast. So remember the sequence: grain, malting, crushing, warm water, and the enzymes turn starch into sugar.

From here the path is familiar. Yeast is added and fermentation begins. For distillation, whisky producers use both pot stills and column stills, although in some cases the law limits their choice. After distillation, whiskies are aged in oak. When maturation is complete they are blended and, where it is allowed and needed, coloured with caramel. Most are then diluted to forty percent alcohol by volume before bottling.

Now, Scotland. All Scotch whisky must be distilled in Scotland and then aged in Scotland for a minimum of three years. Both conditions matter: a spirit made in Scotland but matured somewhere else cannot be called Scotch. Within Scotch there are two important types to know: Single Malt Scotch Whisky and Blended Scotch Whisky.

A Single Malt must meet three conditions. It is made from one hundred percent malted barley, with no other grains. It is distilled in pot stills. And it comes from one distillery. That is what the word single means here: one distillery, not one barrel and not one year. Because they come from pot stills, Single Malts are characterful spirits. On the nose and palate you can find cereal, fruits, flowers and honey and, with time in oak, fruit cake and sweet spices. Two Single Malts from two different distilleries can taste remarkably different.

There is one more flavour sometimes found in these whiskies: smoke. It comes from peat, a natural fuel that is burned when the grains are heated at the end of malting. The smoke from the burning peat flavours the grains, and that flavour travels all the way into the glass. But do not assume every Single Malt is smoky: only a few have peat flavours, although in some of them the smoke is very pronounced.

Scotland also makes a second kind of whisky: grain whisky. It is made from a mix of malted barley and other grains, and it is distilled in a column still. The result has a light aroma intensity and a smooth texture. Grain whisky is hardly ever sold on its own. Its real job is to go into blends.

A Blended Scotch Whisky is a blend of malt whiskies and grain whiskies from different distilleries. Picture an orchestra: the malts are the soloists, intense and full of character, while the light, smooth grain whisky is the string section that holds everything together. Blenders add extra variety by using whiskies of different ages. Blends vary a great deal: some are medium in intensity and fairly simple, others are pronounced and complex. Typically, they are smoother than malt whiskies.

Here is the tip for this lesson. For a Single Malt, count three ones: one grain, malted barley; one kind of still, the pot still; and one distillery. Break any of these and you are no longer looking at a Single Malt. A Blended Scotch, by contrast, mixes malt and grain whiskies from several distilleries.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, grains hold starch, so barley is malted, crushed and mixed with warm water, and its enzymes turn the starch into sugar. Second, every Scotch is distilled and aged for at least three years in Scotland. Third, a Single Malt is one hundred percent malted barley, from pot stills, from one distillery, sometimes smoky from peat; a Blended Scotch mixes malt whiskies with light, column-distilled grain whisky from different distilleries, and is usually smoother.

In the last lesson we stayed in Scotland. Now we cross the Atlantic. In this lesson we meet the three great American whiskeys, Bourbon, Tennessee whiskey and Rye, and see what sets each one apart. Then we take a short tour of three more whisky countries: Ireland, Canada and Japan. You will see that a few simple choices, the grain, the still, the barrel and one unusual filter, explain almost everything.

Let's begin with Bourbon, the best-known American whiskey. Many people link it with Kentucky, and Kentucky is indeed the number one state for production. But Bourbon can be made anywhere in the United States. Its style depends on three factors: the recipe of grains, the way it is distilled, and the type of barrel it is aged in. First, the grains. At least fifty-one percent of the grain used for Bourbon must be corn. The rest is usually made up of barley and rye. Corn brings its typical sweetcorn aromas, and since it is the main grain, those aromas are at the heart of Bourbon's character.

Second, distillation. Bourbon is typically distilled in a column still, but only to a low strength. This is a good reminder of an idea from our first lessons: a column still does not automatically make a light spirit. Stop the distillation at a low strength and plenty of flavour survives. So Bourbon comes out of its column full of character.

Third, the barrel. Bourbon has to be aged in new charred oak barrels, meaning barrels that have never been used and whose insides have been burned. As we know, a new barrel gives the most colour and aroma. Put all three factors together, and Bourbon has pronounced and complex flavours of sweetcorn, cereal, fruit, vanilla and coconut.

A word of warning about one word. People often describe Bourbon as sweet. But Bourbon has no added sugar: it is dry. The vanilla, fruit and coconut aromas make the nose think of desserts, and that is where the confusion comes from. In this course, remember, sweet only means the taste of sugar on the palate.

Now Tennessee whiskey. It can only be made in the state of Tennessee, and it is made in the same way as Bourbon, with one key exception. Before it goes into the barrel, the newly made spirit is passed through a filter of maple charcoal. This charcoal does not make a very fine filter, but it does remove some impurities and helps to give the spirit a smoother character. And note this carefully: the filtering adds no flavour. No maple taste, no smoke.

A simple image helps. Tennessee whiskey is like a Bourbon that takes a shower before going into the barrel. The shower happens to the new, colourless spirit, not to the finished whiskey. After that, the story continues just as it does for Bourbon. Then there is Rye whiskey, Bourbon's spicy cousin. It is made in exactly the same way as Bourbon, except that at least fifty-one percent of the grains used must be rye rather than corn. That single change makes a big difference: rye gives the whiskey spicy and peppery aromas. Where Bourbon leans towards sweetcorn and coconut, Rye has a sharper, livelier edge.

Let's leave America and travel to Ireland. Most Irish whiskeys are made from a blend of pot still and column still spirits, and they are typically light and smooth. There are also pot-distilled whiskeys in Ireland, and some of them use an unusual ingredient: unmalted barley, meaning barley that has not been through malting. It gives a distinctive nutty and oily character.

In Canada, whiskies are made from many different grains, and they are typically a blend of high-strength and low-strength spirits: the high-strength ones are lighter, the low-strength ones bring more flavour. In the best Canadian whiskies, one flavour stands out as a signature: rye, with its spicy, peppery notes.

And Japan. Japanese whisky production was modelled on the industry in Scotland, so Japan makes both malt and blended whiskies. The traditional style is elegant and refined. But new products are increasingly exploring new styles and flavours, so this is a category on the move. Here is the tip for this lesson, a quick way to sort American whiskeys. Mostly corn: Bourbon. Mostly corn plus a maple charcoal shower, made only in Tennessee: Tennessee whiskey. Mostly rye: Rye. And all three share low-strength column distillation and new charred oak.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Bourbon is at least fifty-one percent corn, distilled in a column still to a low strength and aged in new charred oak; it can be made anywhere in the United States, though Kentucky leads, and it is dry. Second, Tennessee whiskey is made like Bourbon but only in Tennessee, with maple charcoal filtering before the barrel, which smooths but adds no flavour; Rye is at least fifty-one percent rye and tastes spicy and peppery. Third, Ireland blends pot and column spirits and sometimes uses unmalted barley, Canada uses many grains with rye as its signature, and Japan follows the Scottish model.

In this lesson we head to the Caribbean to meet rum. Rum is one of the most varied spirit families, from light and discreet to dark and intense, and at first it can seem impossible to sort out. But we have a tool that works every time: the four steps of production. We will look at the two possible raw materials, the fruity aromas that fermentation can build, the choice of still, and everything that can happen after distillation.

The raw material for rum is sugar cane. Sugar cane grows in countries with a hot climate, so that is where rum production is centred, and its classic heartland is the Caribbean. The Caribbean is made up of many small countries, each with its own traditions, rules and regulations. People have tried to classify rum by colour, or by the language spoken where it is made, but neither approach works well. Following the four stages of production is far more useful.

Step one gives the distiller a choice between two raw materials. The first is fresh cane juice. The sugar cane is harvested and crushed to release a sweet juice that can be fermented straight away. Rums made from cane juice often have a very pronounced grassy, herbaceous flavour, a bit like freshly cut grass. The best examples are rhum agricole, which, in the Caribbean, must be made in Martinique or Guadeloupe.

However, most Caribbean distillers use the second option: molasses. Molasses is a black, sticky substance, the by-product of the industry that turns sugar cane juice into sugar. Before fermentation can start, it must be mixed with water. Rums made from molasses have flavours of caramel and brown sugar, rounder and darker than the fresh, green notes of cane juice. So, cane juice means grassy; molasses means caramel and brown sugar.

Step two, fermentation. As always, yeast turns sugar into alcohol, but in rum the fermentation can also be used to create tropical fruit aromas, and sometimes they are very pronounced. When distillers set out to maximise the flavour created during fermentation, the result can be a rum with an intensely fruity set of flavours. Jamaican distillers are well known for producing this style. So when a rum smells strongly of tropical fruit, think fermentation.

Step three, distillation. Most Caribbean distillers can choose which still to use, and that choice decides how intense the rum will be. To create a pronounced, characterful spirit, they might use a pot still. Another option is a short column still, with few sections, which also gives a flavourful spirit; this is the case for rhum agricole.

At the other end of the scale are rums with a light aroma intensity. These are made in tall column stills and distilled to a high strength, which strips away much of the aroma. Examples of this light style can be found in Cuba and Puerto Rico. And many Caribbean distillers own both pot stills and column stills, so they can make several different spirits with different intensities under one roof, like a painter with a full palette of colours.

Step four, after distillation, and here rum offers many paths. Some rums are aged in oak, which gives them colour and aromas of vanilla and sweet spice. In some Caribbean countries a period of oak maturation is even required by law. So how do you make a colourless rum in one of those countries? The distiller uses charcoal filtration, which removes the colour that the oak has given. The result is a white rum that has actually spent time in a barrel.

The other way to make a colourless rum is simply not to use oak at all. The spirit is stored in steel vessels instead. These rums are unaged, and they keep the aromas of the newly made spirit. So a clear rum may be unaged, or it may be aged and then filtered: colour alone cannot tell you which.

When the spirits are ready, they are blended. This is where all that variety pays off: blenders can combine pot still and column still spirits, spirits of different ages, and even spirits from different distilleries, to build the style of each of their brands. Finally, a few last touches. Some rums are sweetened. This is common in Central and South America, but in some countries it is not permitted. Many rums also have their colour adjusted with caramel colour, and some get nearly all of their colour this way. Then, as with almost every spirit, the rum is diluted with water before bottling.

Here is the tip for this lesson: never judge a rum by its colour. A white rum may have spent years in oak before charcoal filtering, and a dark rum may owe its colour mostly to caramel. Instead, walk back through the four steps: cane juice or molasses, how it was fermented, which still, and what happened afterwards.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, rum is made from sugar cane: cane juice gives grassy, herbaceous rums such as rhum agricole from Martinique and Guadeloupe, while molasses, the more common choice, gives caramel and brown sugar flavours. Second, fermentation can build intense tropical fruit, as in Jamaica, and the still decides intensity: pot stills and short columns for character, tall columns for light rums such as those of Cuba and Puerto Rico. Third, rum may be aged or unaged, charcoal-filtered to remove colour, blended, sometimes sweetened and often coloured with caramel.

In this lesson we travel to Mexico to meet Tequila, a spirit with one of the most recognisable aromas on the bar shelf. We will see the plant it comes from and how that plant is turned into a sweet juice, what the words one hundred percent agave really mean, how the best Tequilas are distilled, and the four styles you will find on labels: blanco, joven, reposado and añejo.

Tequila has a very clear identity. It can only be made in certain states of Mexico, and it must be made from the blue agave plant, which is native to Mexico. Picture the plant: a large, hard core surrounded by long, spiky leaves, a little like a giant pineapple sitting in a crown of swords. It is the core that the distiller wants.

Step one, processing the agave. When a plant is harvested, the leaves are cut away, leaving only the hard core. Just like grains, the freshly harvested core has no sugar ready to ferment, so it must be processed to create sugars. This is done by cooking the cores in ovens. Cooking makes them soft and creates sugars inside them. Think of a hard raw potato that becomes soft enough to mash once it has been cooked.

After cooking, the cores are crushed, releasing a sweet juice. And this juice carries the typical aromas of blue agave, a complex range of herbaceous, vegetal, olive, earthy and peppery notes. These are the aromas that make Tequila instantly recognisable, and the rest of the process is largely about deciding how much of them to keep.

Step two, fermentation. The agave juice is mixed with water to create a sugary liquid that can be fermented. At this point the producer has a choice: other sugars, not from agave, can be added to the liquid before fermentation. But there is a firm limit. At least fifty-one percent of the sugars must come from blue agave. In other words, agave must always provide more than half.

This is where an important label term comes in. When a Tequila says one hundred percent agave, it means that only blue agave was used to make the sugary liquid, with no other sugars added. Spirits made only from agave sugars can have a more pronounced agave character. All other Tequilas are simply labelled Tequila. And note that this has nothing to do with age: any Tequila, unaged or aged, can be either Tequila or Tequila one hundred percent agave.

Step three, distillation. Tequila can be made in column stills, but the best Tequilas are double distilled in pot stills, to a notably low strength. Remember our rule: the lower the distillation strength, the more of the raw material's aromas survive. The result is a very distinct and characterful spirit that shows off the herbaceous, peppery aromas of blue agave. It is the exact opposite of vodka, which is distilled to neutral strength precisely to remove aroma.

Step four, after distillation. The distiller can choose whether to age the new spirit in oak or to leave it unaged. When Tequila is oak-aged, it is rarely matured for very long. The aim is balance: some oak aromas of vanilla and spice, without burying the agave character that makes Tequila unique. Oak-aged Tequilas are blended, and caramel colour may be used before they are diluted and bottled.

Now the styles. There are two unaged styles. Blanco, also called silver, is noted for its pure expression of agave flavours: this is agave at its clearest. Then there is joven, also called oro or gold. Despite its golden colour, it is also unaged. Its colour comes from caramel, and its texture is softened with other additives. So a golden Tequila has not necessarily seen a barrel.

There are also two oak-aged styles. Reposado, which means rested, is aged in oak for between two and twelve months. This makes a softer spirit, but it rarely has prominent oak flavours, and it keeps its pronounced agave aromas. Añejo, which means aged, spends at least twelve months in oak barrels, and it shows both agave and oak flavours.

Here is the tip for this lesson. When you read a Tequila label, ask two separate questions. First: how much agave? That is the difference between Tequila, with at least fifty-one percent agave sugars, and one hundred percent agave. Second: how long did it rest? Blanco and joven, none; reposado, two to twelve months; añejo, twelve months or more. The two questions never depend on each other.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Tequila is made in certain Mexican states from blue agave, whose cores are cooked in ovens to create sugars and then crushed, giving herbaceous, vegetal and peppery aromas. Second, at least fifty-one percent of the sugars must come from blue agave, one hundred percent agave means agave only, and the best Tequilas are double distilled in pot stills to a low strength. Third, blanco or silver and joven or gold are unaged, the gold colour coming from caramel; reposado spends two to twelve months in oak, and añejo at least twelve months.

In this lesson we explore flavoured spirits, a big and colourful family that includes flavoured vodka, gin, bitter spirits, cocktail bitters, spiced rum and liqueurs. We will see where these spirits start, the three main ways to add flavour, and what makes each type different. By the end, you will know why a London Dry Gin does not have to come from London, and what separates a liqueur from every other flavoured spirit.

With flavoured spirits, the starting point is unusual. Producers do not have to begin with a raw material at all. In fact, most of them buy in a spirit that has already been made. The vast majority of flavoured spirits are made from the same neutral spirit that is diluted with water to make vodka. Occasionally, rum, whisky or brandy is used as the base instead. So the real craft here lies not in fermenting or distilling, but in adding flavour.

The best flavoured spirits get their flavour from natural ingredients such as fruits, seeds, herbs and spices. Together these are called botanicals. Other flavourings, referred to as artificial flavours, are also used. There are three common ways of adding flavour: redistillation, maceration, and adding ready-made flavourings, natural or artificial. Each method leaves a different mark on the finished spirit.

In redistillation, a diluted neutral spirit is placed in a pot still together with the distiller's chosen botanicals, and the mixture is distilled. What comes out is a flavoured spirit that is colourless. In maceration, the botanicals are simply soaked in the spirit, a little like a cold herbal tea, and their flavours come out over time. This can take a few days or several months: the longer it lasts, the more flavour is extracted, and gently heating the spirit speeds things up. Maceration also gives the spirit colour.

The third method is the simplest. Some producers, normally for reasons of cost, choose not to use botanicals and instead buy in natural or other flavourings. These are very concentrated, so only small quantities are mixed with the spirit to create the final product. To sum up the methods: redistillation gives flavour without colour, maceration gives flavour and colour, and bought-in flavourings give flavour quickly and cheaply.

Let's meet the types, starting with flavoured vodka. It comes in a wide range of flavours: vanilla, fruits such as apple and lemon, and spices such as pepper. Producers typically add bought-in flavourings to their neutral spirit, although some do use redistillation. The result is usually easy to recognise: one clear, direct flavour on a clean, neutral background.

Next, gin. Gin is a flavoured spirit that must have juniper as its predominant flavour. Other common botanicals include coriander seed, angelica root, orris root and citrus peel. Gin is typically made from neutral spirit, although in the United States other distilled spirits can be used. Flavour can be added by redistillation, or producers can simply add bought-in flavourings. The best gins are usually redistilled, although some very delicate flavours are added after distillation. Gins are typically unaged and colourless.

Now a classic exam point. The popular labelling term London Dry Gin indicates that the flavours were added during redistillation. It is a method, not a place: London Dry Gin can be made anywhere in the world. It does not have to be made in London. So when you see London Dry on a label, think of the method, not of the city: a London Dry Gin made on another continent is perfectly possible.

Bitter spirits are made with at least one bitter botanical, such as gentian, quinine or bitter orange. Here is an interesting detail: the bitterness can only be detected on the palate, not on the nose. The aroma comes from the bitter botanicals and from many others besides. Traditionally these spirits were drunk at the beginning or the end of a meal, but today they are mostly used in cocktails. Cocktail bitters are something different again: highly concentrated and intensely bitter spirits. Nobody drinks them on their own. Instead, they are used in tiny quantities, a dash or two, to give cocktails extra complexity, rather like salt and pepper in cooking.

Spiced rum is a very varied category, both in the base rum and in the flavourings added. Some are made from a light, unaged rum that is flavoured and coloured with caramel. Only a handful are based on oak-aged rums. Both botanicals and other flavourings are used. So, once again, an amber colour does not prove years in a barrel.

Finally, liqueurs. A liqueur is a flavoured spirit that has also been sweetened. Most are made from neutral spirit, but some start from characterful spirits such as brandy, rum or whisky. There is no limit to the flavours that can be used, or to the methods of adding them, and one notable ingredient found in some liqueurs is cream. Sugar is added after flavouring, and by law a liqueur must reach a minimum level of sweetness. Many are also coloured: natural colour from maceration can fade quickly, so artificial colours are widely used to keep the colour stable and to offer a broader, often vivid, range of shades.

Here is the tip for this lesson: a liqueur is flavour plus sugar. Gin, flavoured vodka and bitter spirits are flavoured too, but only a liqueur must, by law, be sweet. And for gin, remember that London Dry describes how it is made, not where. A quick check: if a spirit is flavoured but not sweet, it is not a liqueur.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, most flavoured spirits start from a bought-in neutral spirit, and flavour is added by redistillation, which keeps the spirit colourless, by maceration, which adds colour, or with bought-in flavourings. Second, gin must taste mainly of juniper, and London Dry means flavours added by redistillation, anywhere in the world; bitter spirits have at least one bitter botanical, cocktail bitters are used in tiny amounts, and spiced rum is often a light rum plus flavourings and caramel. Third, a liqueur is a flavoured spirit sweetened to a legal minimum, in any flavour, even cream, and is often coloured.

In this lesson we look at a family that is not, strictly speaking, made of spirits at all: aromatised wines. So why do they belong in a spirits course? Because you will find them on almost every bar, and they are some of the most useful ingredients in cocktails. We will see the four components that every aromatised wine shares, what each one does, where these wines are best known, and the rules that define the most famous of them: vermouth.

Aromatised wines are a diverse category, with many recipes and styles. Yet they are all built from the same four components: a base wine, flavourings that always include something bitter, sugar, and a spirit. A fifth ingredient, caramel colour, is sometimes used as well. Think of a stool with four legs: wine, bitterness, sweetness and spirit. Take one away, and the whole thing wobbles.

Let's start with the base wine. Most aromatised wines are made from a white wine. Most producers choose a relatively neutral wine, which works as a blank canvas to show off the added flavours. Others prefer aromatic wines, and then balance the wine's own aromas with their choice of flavourings. There are also aromatised wines made from red or rosé wine, but white is by far the most common base.

Second component: the spirit. A small quantity of spirit must be added to every aromatised wine. There are two reasons. It raises the level of alcohol, and it gives the product a longer shelf life, especially once the bottle has been opened. The spirit chosen is nearly always neutral, so that it adds strength without getting in the way of the flavours.

Third component: the flavourings. They can be added directly to the wine, or in the form of flavoured spirits. The recipes are extremely varied, but they all have one feature in common: they use bitter botanicals. The classic examples are wormwood, gentian and quinine. You may recognise gentian and quinine from our lesson on bitter spirits: the same bitter family turns up again here.

Fourth component: sugar. Almost no aromatised wines are completely dry. The sweetness can come from the wine itself or from sugar added by the producer. This sweetness is what balances the bitterness of the botanicals, and together they give aromatised wines their characteristic bittersweet taste. Bitter without sweet would be harsh; sweet without bitter would be dull.

And the optional extra: caramel colour. It is not always used, but it plays an important role in red vermouths. These are made from a white wine base, so their red or brown colour does not come from the grapes: it is given by caramel. In this case, caramel can also add aromas of caramel to the drink. So a red vermouth is not, as many people assume, a red wine with herbs.

Where are aromatised wines made? They can be made anywhere in the world, but the best-known areas of production are south-east France and north-west Italy. In both countries, the most widely made type of aromatised wine is vermouth. Vermouth follows two rules. It is made from a white wine base, and it must be flavoured with wormwood, a strongly bitter botanical. Wormwood is the botanical that defines every vermouth. Beyond that, each producer builds their own recipe of herbs, spices and other botanicals.

Now, a couple of label traps. A vermouth labelled dry is almost never truly dry: it nearly always has some added sugar, just less than other styles. Red vermouths, on the other hand, are typically heavily sweetened. So in vermouth, the word dry means less sweet, not without sugar. Read the style on the label, and expect some sweetness in every bottle.

Why do bartenders love aromatised wines? Because a single ingredient can bring three things to a cocktail at once: sweetness, bitterness and acidity. Acidity comes from the wine, bitterness from the botanicals, sweetness from the sugar. That is why you will meet vermouth again in some of the great classics we will study in the cocktail lessons, from the Manhattan to the Martini and the Negroni.

Here is the tip for this lesson: vermouth equals white wine plus wormwood, and even a dry vermouth carries a little sugar. If you also remember the four-legged stool, wine, bitterness, sugar and spirit, you can describe any aromatised wine. And remember that a red vermouth owes its colour to caramel, not to red wine.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, aromatised wines are not spirits, but every one is built from a base wine, flavourings that always include something bitter, sugar and a small amount of usually neutral spirit, with caramel as an option. Second, the base is usually a fairly neutral white wine, the spirit raises alcohol and lengthens shelf life, and almost none are fully dry. Third, the best-known areas are south-east France and north-west Italy, where the main type is vermouth: a white wine base with wormwood, where even dry has sugar and red is heavily sweetened and coloured with caramel.

In this lesson we learn how to taste a spirit properly. Not how to enjoy a glass with friends, but how to look at a spirit closely, describe it accurately and write notes you can trust. We will see how to prepare the room, the glass and yourself, the step-by-step method for tasting, and what to write down for appearance, nose, palate and finish.

The key word is consistency. If you take exactly the same approach with every sample, your notes will describe each spirit accurately, and you will be able to compare them, even months later. A note written today should mean the same thing as a note written next year. So the method matters as much as the spirit in the glass.

Start with the setting. There should be no distracting smells in the room: no perfume, no cooking, no scented candles. You need a good source of natural light, and a white surface, such as a sheet of paper or a white tablecloth, to help you judge the colour of the spirit without misleading reflections.

Then the glass. Choose one with a wide bowl that narrows towards the top, a little like a tulip. The wide bowl gives the aromas room to gather, and the narrower opening concentrates them and channels them towards your nose, which makes the nose much easier to assess. In a straight, open glass, the aromas simply drift away.

And finally, the taster. Your palate should be clean, with no lingering flavours, so no toothpaste or coffee just before a tasting. And you should be well hydrated. Treat it like preparing an instrument before a concert: if the instrument is not ready, even the best music sounds wrong.

Now the method. Remember that spirits, even after the distiller has diluted them, are still very strong drinks. At forty percent alcohol by volume, it is not easy to make a fully accurate assessment: the alcohol stings the nose and can numb the palate. So the recommended approach uses a small sample and some water.

Pour a small sample of one and a half centilitres, that is about half a US fluid ounce, roughly a tablespoon. First, look at it and assess its appearance. Then smell it and assess the nose, while it is still neat. Only after that do you add water: the same amount again, one and a half centilitres. This halves the strength of the sample.

Now smell the spirit again. With less alcohol in the way, aromas that were hidden often appear, like opening a window in a crowded room. Next, assess the palate: take a small sip, let it move around your mouth and look for the flavours. Then spit. Spitting is completely normal in a tasting: it keeps your head clear, so you can judge the last sample as carefully as the first.

So, what do you write down? The notes follow the same order: appearance, nose, palate. For appearance, you only need the colour. The main scale goes from colourless to lemon, gold, amber and brown. Unaged spirits are usually colourless, while oak-aged ones move along that scale. Some spirits, especially flavoured spirits and liqueurs, can show other colours: pink, red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, even black.

On the nose, first judge the intensity: neutral, light, medium or pronounced. A neutral vodka sits at one end, an intense rum or a peaty whisky at the other. Then describe the aromas, and it helps to group them by where they come from: the raw material, such as grape, grain, cane or agave; the processing, such as fruity notes from fermentation; and oak and maturation, such as vanilla, spice or dried fruit.

On the palate, you look for the same groups of flavours: raw material, processing, oak and maturation. You also note other observations, in particular the sugar level, whether the spirit is dry or sweet, and the texture, for example light and smooth or richer and oily. Finally, the finish: what stays after you have spat. Judge its length, short, medium or long, and its character: neutral, simple, some complexity or very complex. A very complex finish keeps offering new flavours, one after another, long after the sip has gone.

Here is the tip for this lesson, a little rhyme for the method: pour a little, look and sniff, add the same in water, sniff again, then taste and spit. And remember: the same amount of water as spirit, every time, so that every note you write is comparable. Write your notes as you go, while each impression is still fresh.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, prepare the conditions: no distracting smells, natural light, a white surface, a glass with a wide bowl that narrows at the top, a clean palate and good hydration. Second, follow the method: a small sample of about one and a half centilitres, look and smell, add the same amount of water, smell again, taste, then spit. Third, write down the colour, the nose intensity from neutral to pronounced, the aromas grouped by source, the palate with sugar and texture, and the finish with its length and complexity.

In this lesson we step behind the bar. Before we learn any recipes, we need the principle that sits underneath all of them: balance. We will look at the two sets of scales that every cocktail is built on, strong against weak, and sweet against bitter or sour, and then at the first big division of the cocktail world: short drinks and long drinks. With these ideas, hundreds of recipes suddenly become much easier to understand.

What makes a great cocktail? Good-quality ingredients and the right tools certainly help. But what really separates a good cocktail from a great one is balance, and a balanced cocktail shares many of the qualities we look for in a fine spirit. Generally speaking, two sets of scales are used to achieve it. The first weighs strong against weak. The second weighs sweet against bitter, sour, or both.

Let's start with the strong side. The strong element of a cocktail is the base spirit. It is generally forty percent alcohol by volume or higher, and it is the centrepiece of the flavour: the rum in a Daiquiri, the gin in a Martini, the whiskey in an Old Fashioned. The rest of the drink is built around it.

The weak side softens that strength. One source of weakness is always there: ice. When a cocktail is stirred or shaken with ice, some of it melts and dilutes the drink. Other weak ingredients are optional and non-alcoholic: fruit juices, dairy products such as cream, sodas, club soda and tonic. Think of a gin and tonic: the gin is the strong part, while the tonic and the ice bring the weak part.

Change the strong element and you change the drink. Even using a different brand of spirit from the same category can alter a cocktail. A more radical change is to replace the strong component with a completely different spirit. For example, make an Old Fashioned with rum instead of whiskey, and you have a rum Old Fashioned: same structure, new character.

Now the second set of scales. It is very common for a cocktail to be sweetened, and then seasoned with another ingredient, called a modifier, which provides a bitter or sour counterpoint, or both. Sweetness can come in many forms: plain sugar, simple syrup, which is just sugar dissolved in water, or liqueurs. But beware: if a cocktail is too sweet, it becomes cloying and unpleasant.

So the sweetness has to be balanced. On one side there are sour ingredients, which means acidic ones, above all citrus juices such as lemon and lime. On the other side there are bitter ingredients, most obviously cocktail bitters, added by the dash. It works just like cooking: a squeeze of lemon or a pinch of salt can lift a dish that tasted flat and heavy.

Remember too that a single ingredient can provide several of these elements at once. Aromatised wines such as vermouth are the perfect example: they bring sweetness, bitterness and acidity in one pour. The key to success is to balance strong against weak, and sweet against bitter and sour, so that the result is a cohesive whole where no single component dominates the others.

Put the two scales together and you get the four points of balance: strong, weak, sweet, and bitter or sour. Every cocktail is built from these four. Once you understand them, a bartender can adjust any recipe as needed, adding a little more citrus to a drink that is too sweet, or a little more dilution to a drink that is too strong.

Now the first big division: short drinks and long drinks. Short drinks usually have a limited number of ingredients, and they rely on dilution from shaking or stirring with ice to provide the weak component. They are small and concentrated. Within this category there are two families: the spirit-forward cocktail, where the spirit takes centre stage, and the short sour, built on spirit, citrus and sweetness.

Long drinks are typically larger, with a higher volume. Their weak component is often provided by sodas, juices, dairy products or other non-alcoholic drinks. Within this category there are two families: the highball, the simplest of all mixed drinks, and the long sour. We will meet all four families, with their classic recipes, in the next lesson.

Short and long drinks are closely related. Take a short sour of gin, lemon juice and simple syrup. Pour it over ice and top it with club soda, and it becomes a long drink, a Tom Collins. The core ingredients stay the same; what changes is the amount of the weak part, and with it the volume and the strength.

Here is the tip for this lesson: think of a cocktail as a dish to season. The spirit is the main ingredient, ice and mixers are the water in the pot, sugar is the sweetness, and citrus and bitters are the salt and lemon that bring it to life. If one flavour shouts louder than the others, the dish is not balanced yet.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, balance uses two sets of scales: strong against weak, and sweet against bitter, sour or both. Second, the strong part is the base spirit, usually forty percent or more; the weak part is dilution from ice, plus juices, dairy, sodas or tonic; sweetness comes from sugar, simple syrup or liqueurs, and is balanced by citrus or bitters, while aromatised wines can bring all three at once. Third, short drinks rely on ice dilution and include spirit-forward cocktails and short sours; long drinks are lengthened with mixers and include highballs and long sours.

In this last lesson we meet the classic cocktail families. There are hundreds of classic cocktails, and new ones are invented all the time, so the cocktail world can look overwhelming. In fact, it is not. Most classics belong to one of four families: the spirit-forward cocktail and the short sour, which are short drinks, and the highball and the long sour, which are long drinks. Let's see how each family works, and which famous drinks belong to it.

First, the spirit-forward cocktail. These drinks are higher in alcohol than the others, and they celebrate their strong ingredient. In their simplest form they combine a spirit with sugar and bitters, or a spirit with a liqueur. In more complex versions, sweetness and bitterness are balanced with various combinations of sugar, aromatised wines and bitters. They are generally built in the glass or stirred, and the ice provides both dilution and chilling.

The Old Fashioned is the model: Bourbon, a sugar cube and aromatic bitters. The Manhattan uses rye whiskey or Bourbon with the same kind of aromatic bitters, but the sweetness comes from sweet vermouth, whose complexity makes it quite distinct from the Old Fashioned. The Sazerac takes Cognac or rye whiskey, sugar, a different style of cocktail bitters and a touch of absinthe. And the Rusty Nail is the simplest of all: Scotch whisky with a whisky-based honey liqueur.

Gin gives two more great classics. The Martini combines gin with dry vermouth, which on its own brings both the bitter and the sweet element. The Negroni combines gin, sweet vermouth and a red bitter spirit: three ingredients, three clear roles. One more modification is worth knowing: adding cream creates the Alexander family of cocktails, such as the Brandy Alexander.

Second family: the short sour. It is built on a classic balance of strong, sour and sweet. A classic sour uses a spirit, a citrus juice, and an unflavoured sweetener such as simple syrup. These drinks are shaken: shaking chills and mixes the ingredients, adds some dilution, and creates a light, airy texture. Some recipes also call for egg white, which gives a foam head and a silky texture. Many bars now use vegan alternatives such as aquafaba, the water chickpeas are cooked in.

Three classics show the pure formula. The Daiquiri: rum, lime juice and simple syrup. The Whiskey Sour: Bourbon or rye whiskey, lemon juice and simple syrup, with optional egg white and bitters. And the Pisco Sour, made with pisco, a grape brandy: pisco, lime juice and simple syrup, plus one egg white and a dash of bitters. In the Pisco Sour, the egg white is essential.

More complex sours change the formula by using a flavoured sweetener, a different sour ingredient, or both. The Sidecar: Cognac, lemon juice and triple sec, an orange liqueur, in place of the syrup. The Margarita: Tequila, lime juice and triple sec, with an optional salt rim. And the Clover Club: gin, lemon juice and raspberry syrup, with egg white and an optional touch of vermouth.

Third family: the highball, the simplest of all mixed drinks. It is a long drink, a spirit with a non-alcoholic mixer, served over cubed ice. Gin and tonic, vodka and tonic, and whisky and soda are obvious examples. Some highballs have their own names. The Cuba Libre is rum and cola with lime. The Greyhound is vodka and grapefruit juice.

Some highballs go a little further. The Horse's Neck adds bitters to a spirit and a mixer: Cognac, ginger ale and bitters. Others use a split base for the strong element. The Americano is the classic example: its strong part is shared between a red bitter spirit and sweet vermouth, topped with club soda.

Fourth family: the long sour, which includes several sub-categories: the Collins, the Sling and the sparkling sour. In their simplest form, they are just short sours turned into long drinks by adding club soda. The Tom Collins is the perfect example: gin, lemon juice and simple syrup, topped with club soda.

The club soda can be swapped for something else. In a Paloma, it becomes a flavoured soda: Tequila and lime juice with a Mexican grapefruit soda, or alternatively grapefruit juice mixed with soda. In a French 75, it becomes Champagne: Cognac or gin, lemon juice and simple syrup, topped with Champagne. That is a sparkling sour.

Other long sours are enhanced with extra ingredients. Sometimes it is simple, as in the Mojito: rum, lime juice, sugar or simple syrup and mint leaves, topped with soda water. Sometimes it is more complex, as in the Singapore Sling: gin and lime juice, sweetened with a cherry liqueur and a herbal liqueur, with a dash of aromatic bitters and a top of club soda.

Here is the tip for this lesson. To place any cocktail, ask two questions. Is it short or long? And is it built around the spirit, or around citrus? Short and spirit-led: spirit-forward. Short with citrus: short sour. Long with just a mixer: highball. Long with citrus: long sour. Then remember the four points of balance: strong, weak, sweet, and bitter or sour.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, spirit-forward cocktails are the strongest, built or stirred: Old Fashioned, Manhattan, Sazerac, Rusty Nail, Martini and Negroni, with cream giving the Alexander family. Second, short sours are spirit, citrus and sweetener, shaken: Daiquiri, Whiskey Sour and Pisco Sour, with egg white essential in the Pisco Sour, and variations such as the Sidecar, Margarita and Clover Club. Third, highballs are a spirit and a mixer over ice, such as the Cuba Libre, Greyhound, Horse's Neck and Americano, while long sours are lengthened sours, such as the Tom Collins, Paloma, French 75, Mojito and Singapore Sling.
